nodeData.note: Technical track · Linear algebra, probability and statistics, calculus and optimisation — just what AI needs.

children.note: Linear algebra is the maths of lists and grids of numbers. Almost everything an AI model stores and computes, from word meanings to neural network layers, is written as vectors and matrices, so this is the first maths to get comfortable with.

AI works with uncertain, noisy data and gives answers that are guesses with some chance of being wrong. Probability is the language for that uncertainty, and statistics is how we learn from data and judge how much to trust the result.
Training an AI model means nudging millions of numbers so that its errors shrink. Calculus tells you which way to nudge each number, and optimisation is the step-by-step process of doing it.

nodeData.note: Linear algebra is the maths of lists and grids of numbers. Almost everything an AI model stores and computes, from word meanings to neural network layers, is written as vectors and matrices, so this is the first maths to get comfortable with.

children.note: Before matrices, start with the vector: an ordered list of numbers that can describe anything measurable.
A scalar is one number, a vector is a 1-D list, a matrix is a 2-D grid, and a tensor is the general name for arrays with any number of axes. Deep learning libraries call all of them tensors.

manas.q: What is the difference between a scalar, vector, matrix and tensor?

children.topic: A vector is an ordered list
children.note: A vector such as [3, 1, 4] holds numbers in a fixed order, and position matters: the first entry always means the same feature. Example: a patient could be [age, weight, blood pressure].

manas.q: What is a vector, in AI terms?

children.note: In 2-D or 3-D you can draw a vector as an arrow from the origin. Its direction tells you which way it points and its length tells you how big it is. The same ideas carry over to 1,000 dimensions, even though we cannot draw them.
A vector with n numbers lives in n-dimensional space. A grayscale 28×28 image flattened into one list is a 784-dimensional vector.

manas.q: How many dimensions does a flattened 28×28 grayscale image have?

children.note: Add two vectors entry by entry: [1, 2] + [3, 4] = [4, 6]. Multiply by a number to stretch it: 2 × [1, 2] = [2, 4]. "Linear" means built only from these two moves.
The usual length is the square root of the sum of squares: ||v|| = √(v1² + v2² + … + vn²). For [3, 4] the length is 5. Norms also measure how big model weights are.

manas.q: What is the length (L2 norm) of the vector [3, 4]?

children.note: Dividing a vector by its own length gives a unit vector of length 1 that keeps the direction. Normalising lets you compare directions without size getting in the way.
The dot product turns two vectors into one number that says how much they point the same way. It is the single most common operation in AI.
Multiply matching entries and add them up: a·b = a1b1 + a2b2 + … + anbn. Example: [1, 2, 3]·[4, 5, 6] = 4 + 10 + 18 = 32. Both vectors must have the same length.
The dot product also equals |a| × |b| × cos θ, where θ is the angle between the arrows. So it combines how long the vectors are with how closely they line up.
A positive dot product means the vectors point roughly the same way, zero means they are at right angles, and negative means they point in opposite directions.
Two vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular) when their dot product is exactly 0. Orthogonal directions carry completely separate information.

manas.q: What does a dot product of exactly zero tell you?

children.note: Cosine similarity = a·b / (|a| × |b|). It ignores length and keeps only direction, giving a score from −1 to 1. Search engines and chatbots use it to find the text closest in meaning to a question.

manas.q: What does cosine similarity measure, and what is its range?

children.topic: A neuron is a dot product
children.note: An artificial neuron computes y = w·x + b: the dot product of its weights w with the input x, plus a bias b, then passes it through an activation function. Learning means adjusting w and b.

manas.q: What calculation does a single artificial neuron do before its activation function?

children.note: A matrix is a grid of numbers. It can hold a whole dataset, or act as a machine that transforms vectors, which is exactly what a neural network layer does.
A matrix with m rows and n columns has shape m×n. In a dataset, rows are usually examples (patients, farms, sentences) and columns are features.

manas.q: What does the shape m×n of a matrix mean?

children.note: Multiplying a vector by a matrix can rotate, stretch, squash or project it. Thinking of a matrix as a transformation, not just a table, is the key intuition.
Each output entry is the dot product of one matrix row with the vector. A 3×4 matrix turns a 4-number input into a 3-number output.
You can multiply A (m×n) by B (n×p) only when the inner sizes match; the result is m×p. Entry (i, j) of the product is row i of A dotted with column j of B.

manas.q: If A is 32×128 and B is 128×10, what is the shape of AB?

children.note: Matrix multiplication is usually not commutative: AB and BA can differ, or one may not even exist. Applying transformations in a different order gives a different result.

manas.q: Is matrix multiplication commutative?

children.note: The identity matrix I has 1s on the diagonal and leaves vectors unchanged. The transpose Aᵀ swaps rows and columns, turning an m×n matrix into n×m.

manas.q: What does transposing a matrix do?

children.note: A fully connected layer is one matrix-vector product plus a bias vector. Stack many layers with activation functions between them and you have a deep network.
Put a batch of inputs as rows of a matrix X and one multiplication X Wᵀ processes them all together. This is why training works in batches.
In NumPy or PyTorch, write C = A @ B for matrix multiplication. A * B is different: it multiplies entry by entry.
Most early bugs in AI code are linear algebra bugs.
An error like "shapes (3,4) and (3,4) not aligned" means the inner sizes do not match. Print .shape of every array when debugging.
Element-wise (*) multiplies matching entries; matrix product (@) does row-by-column dot products. Mixing them up gives wrong answers, sometimes silently.

manas.q: In NumPy, what is the difference between A * B and A @ B?

children.note: Comparing raw dot products favours long vectors. Normalise first, or use cosine similarity, when you only care about direction.
Modern AI turns words, images, songs or users into vectors called embeddings, so that "similar meaning" becomes "nearby in space".
An embedding is a learned list of numbers that represents an item. The model learns the numbers during training so that useful relationships show up as geometry.

manas.q: What is an embedding?

children.note: Good embeddings place "doctor" near "nurse" and "maize" near "wheat". Distance or cosine similarity then measures how related two items are.
A well-known word2vec example: the vector for king − man + woman lands near queen. Such neat patterns appear sometimes, not always, and should not be over-read.
A language model stores one row per token in an embedding matrix. Looking up a token simply means picking its row, which then flows through the network.

manas.q: How does a language model turn a token into a vector?

children.note: Real embeddings commonly have hundreds to a few thousand dimensions. More dimensions can hold finer distinctions but cost memory and compute.
To search by meaning, embed every document once, embed the question, and return the documents with the highest cosine similarity. Retrieval-augmented chatbots work this way.
A vector database stores millions of embeddings and finds nearest neighbours quickly, usually with approximate search methods that trade a little accuracy for speed.

children.topic: Limits: bias lives in the geometry
children.note: Embeddings learn from human text, so they can encode stereotypes, for example linking jobs to one gender. Measure and test them before trusting them.

manas.q: Why can embeddings be biased?

children.note: Eigenvectors reveal the directions a matrix treats specially. You will meet them in data compression, PCA and analysis of trained models.
An eigenvector v of matrix A keeps its direction when transformed: Av = λv. The number λ is the eigenvalue, the factor by which v is stretched or flipped.

manas.q: What equation defines an eigenvector v and eigenvalue λ of matrix A?

children.topic: Picture: the axes that do not turn
children.note: Most vectors get knocked off their line by a transformation. Eigenvectors stay on their own line, only getting longer, shorter or reversed.
Principal component analysis finds the eigenvectors of the data covariance matrix. The top ones point where the data varies most, so you can keep a few and drop the rest.

manas.q: What does PCA use eigenvectors for?

children.note: Singular value decomposition splits any matrix into rotation × stretch × rotation. It powers compression, recommender systems and noise removal.
A low-rank matrix can be written as the product of two thin matrices, using far fewer numbers. Fine-tuning methods such as LoRA train small low-rank updates instead of the full weight matrix.
Training and running AI is dominated by huge matrix multiplications. Graphics chips were built for exactly this kind of repetitive, parallel arithmetic.
Every entry of a matrix product can be computed separately from the others. That makes the work easy to split across thousands of small cores at once.

manas.q: Why is matrix multiplication well suited to GPUs?

children.note: A CPU has a few powerful cores good at varied, step-by-step tasks. A GPU has thousands of simpler cores that do the same operation on lots of data in parallel.
In large neural networks, most of the compute during training and use goes into matrix multiplications in the layers and attention.

manas.q: Which operation uses most of the compute in large neural networks?

children.note: Modern GPUs include units dedicated to small matrix multiplications, and Google built TPUs for the same job. Other chip makers offer similar accelerators.
Using 16-bit or 8-bit numbers instead of 32-bit lets chips do more multiplications per second and use less memory, usually with little loss in quality.
Moving numbers in and out of memory can take longer than the arithmetic itself. Good AI code keeps data on the GPU and reuses it.

nodeData.note: AI works with uncertain, noisy data and gives answers that are guesses with some chance of being wrong. Probability is the language for that uncertainty, and statistics is how we learn from data and judge how much to trust the result.

children.note: The core vocabulary: chances, events, random variables and how one event changes the chance of another.
0 means impossible, 1 means certain, 0.5 means as likely as not. Probabilities of all possible outcomes must add up to 1.

manas.q: What range must every probability fall in?

children.note: A classifier does not just say "malaria"; it gives, say, 0.82 for malaria and 0.18 for not. A language model gives a probability for every possible next token.
A random variable is a quantity whose value depends on chance, such as tomorrow's rainfall in Kisumu or the number of patients at a clinic today.
P(A | B) is the chance of A given that B is known to be true. P(rain | dark clouds) is higher than P(rain) on a random day.

manas.q: What does P(A | B) mean?

children.note: A and B are independent if knowing one tells you nothing about the other: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Two fair coin flips are independent.

manas.q: When are two events independent?

children.note: The joint probability P(A, B) covers both happening together. Summing a joint table over one variable gives the marginal probability of the other.
A distribution describes all the values something can take and how likely each is. A few numbers like the mean and variance summarise it.
A probability distribution assigns chances to every possible outcome. It is the full picture; averages are just summaries of it.

manas.q: What is a probability distribution?

children.note: Discrete variables take separate values (number of children). Continuous ones take any value in a range (height). Continuous distributions use a density curve.
For continuous variables, probability is the area under the density curve over a range. A density value itself can be bigger than 1.
A handful of named distributions appear again and again in AI.
Bernoulli is one yes/no trial with chance p. Binomial counts the yeses in n independent trials, such as how many of 20 seeds sprout.
The bell curve, set by its mean and standard deviation. Many measurements are roughly normal, and it is used to initialise neural network weights.

manas.q: Which two numbers define a normal distribution?

children.note: Every value in a range is equally likely, like a fair die. Often used as a neutral starting assumption or for random initialisation.
One outcome out of k options, each with its own probability. A language model's next-token output is a categorical distribution over its vocabulary.

manas.q: What kind of distribution does a language model output for the next token?

children.note: Centre and spread are the two summaries you will use most.
The mean is the average: add the values and divide by how many there are. The expected value is the long-run average of a random variable.

manas.q: What is the expected value of a random variable?

children.note: The middle value when data is sorted. It resists outliers: one billionaire barely moves the median income but drags the mean up.
Variance is the average squared distance from the mean: Var = mean of (x − μ)². Standard deviation is its square root, in the same units as the data.

manas.q: How are variance and standard deviation related?

children.note: For a normal distribution about 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2 and 99.7% within 3.

manas.q: In a normal distribution, roughly what share of values lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean?

children.note: Bayes' rule tells you how to update a belief when new evidence arrives. It is the backbone of reasoning under uncertainty.
P(H | E) = P(E | H) × P(H) / P(E). It turns "how likely is the evidence if the hypothesis is true" into "how likely is the hypothesis now that I have seen the evidence".

manas.q: State Bayes' rule.

children.note: The prior P(H) is your belief before evidence. The likelihood P(E | H) is how well H explains the evidence. The posterior P(H | E) is your updated belief.

manas.q: What are the prior and the posterior in Bayes' rule?

children.note: A disease affects 1% of people. A test catches 90% of cases but wrongly flags 9% of healthy people. Of everyone testing positive, only about 9% actually have the disease.

manas.q: Why can a positive result from a fairly accurate test still mean a low chance of disease?

children.note: Ignoring how rare something is to begin with is a common reasoning error. A model screening for a rare condition will raise many false alarms unless this is accounted for.
A simple classifier that applies Bayes' rule while assuming features are independent given the class. Despite that crude assumption it works well for tasks like spam filtering.
Bayesian methods keep a whole distribution over model parameters instead of one best value, which gives a natural measure of uncertainty, at extra computing cost.
Most model training is a search for the parameters that make the observed data most probable.
Probability fixes the model and asks how likely different data are. Likelihood fixes the observed data and asks how well different parameter values explain it.

manas.q: What is the difference between probability and likelihood?

children.note: MLE picks the parameter values under which the observed data would be most likely. Many training methods are MLE in disguise.

manas.q: What does maximum likelihood estimation choose?

children.note: You see 7 heads in 10 flips. The likelihood of the data is highest when the coin's heads chance p = 0.7, so 0.7 is the maximum likelihood estimate.
Multiplying many small probabilities underflows to zero on a computer. Taking logs turns the product into a sum, which is stable and easier to optimise.
For classification and language models, the usual loss is the negative log of the probability given to the correct answer. Minimising it is the same as maximising likelihood.

manas.q: How is cross-entropy loss related to likelihood?

children.topic: Sampling: from data and from models
children.note: We learn from samples of the world, and generative models produce outputs by sampling. Both need care.
The population is everything you care about; a sample is the part you actually measured. Statistics is about saying something reliable about the population from the sample.

manas.q: What is the difference between a population and a sample?

children.note: If the sample is not representative, conclusions do not transfer. A skin-condition model trained mostly on light skin may fail on dark skin.
As a sample grows, its average gets closer to the true average. Small samples bounce around a lot.
Averages of many independent samples tend toward a normal distribution, whatever the original shape. This is why the bell curve shows up so often.

manas.q: What does the central limit theorem say?

children.note: Randomly split data so the model is judged on examples it never saw. The test set estimates how it will do on new data from the same source.
Chatbots sample the next token from a distribution. Low temperature sharpens it toward the top choice; high temperature flattens it for more variety and more mistakes.

manas.q: What does raising the sampling temperature do to a language model's output?

children.note: When exact maths is too hard, simulate many random samples and average the results. Used for estimating risk, integrals and uncertainty.
Knowing how strongly things move together is useful; knowing what causes what, and how sure you are, is harder.
Pearson correlation runs from −1 to 1. Near 1 means the two rise together, near −1 means one falls as the other rises, near 0 means no straight-line link.

manas.q: What range does the Pearson correlation coefficient take?

children.note: Two things moving together does not prove one causes the other. Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in hot weather; heat drives both.

manas.q: Why does correlation not prove causation?

children.note: A confounder is a hidden third factor that affects both variables. Models trained on observational data happily learn confounded shortcuts.
Randomly assigning a treatment breaks the link with confounders, which is why randomised controlled trials are the strongest evidence of cause.
A 95% confidence interval comes from a method that captures the true value in about 95% of repeated samples. Narrow intervals need more data.

manas.q: What does a 95% confidence interval mean?

children.note: A p-value is how surprising the data would be if there were truly no effect. A small p-value is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
A model is calibrated if, among predictions made with 80% confidence, about 80% are right. Many modern networks are overconfident, so check before trusting the numbers.

manas.q: What does it mean for a model to be well calibrated?

children.note: Clear visual explanations of the key ideas.

nodeData.note: Training an AI model means nudging millions of numbers so that its errors shrink. Calculus tells you which way to nudge each number, and optimisation is the step-by-step process of doing it.

children.note: A derivative tells you how fast one quantity changes when you change another a tiny bit. It is the basic tool behind all model training.
A model's error depends on its parameters. If you know how the error changes as each parameter moves, you know how to improve the model.
The derivative f'(x) is the slope of the curve at x: how much f changes per small step in x. Positive slope means going up, negative means going down.

manas.q: What does the derivative of a function tell you at a point?

children.note: f'(x) is the limit of (f(x + h) − f(x)) / h as the step h shrinks toward zero. It is the "instant" rate of change.
The derivative of f(x) = x² is 2x. At x = 3 the slope is 6, so a small step to the right raises f about 6 times as much as the step.

manas.q: What is the derivative of x², and its value at x = 3?

children.note: Power rule: xⁿ → n·xⁿ⁻¹. Constants drop out. The derivative of a sum is the sum of derivatives. With these you can handle most simple formulas.
At the bottom of a valley or top of a hill, the derivative is zero. Optimisation is largely a hunt for low points where the slope flattens.

manas.q: What is the derivative at the bottom of a smooth valley?

children.note: You can estimate a derivative numerically: (f(x + h) − f(x − h)) / 2h with a small h. Programmers use this to check that gradient code is correct.
Real models have millions of parameters. The gradient collects every slope into one vector.
A partial derivative measures change in one input while holding the others fixed, written ∂f/∂x. For f(x, y) = x² + 3y, ∂f/∂x = 2x and ∂f/∂y = 3.

manas.q: What is a partial derivative?

children.note: The gradient ∇f lists all partial derivatives: ∇f = [∂f/∂x1, …, ∂f/∂xn]. It has one entry per parameter.

manas.q: What is the gradient of a function?

children.note: The gradient points in the direction where the function rises fastest. Walking the opposite way is the fastest local way down.

manas.q: In which direction does the gradient point?

children.note: A large gradient means the surface is steep here; a tiny gradient means it is nearly flat, which can mean you are near a minimum or just stuck on a plateau.
Picture a hiking map with height lines. The gradient is always at right angles to the contour lines, pointing toward higher ground.
Neural networks are functions inside functions. The chain rule tells you how to get derivatives through every layer.
If y depends on u and u depends on x, then dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx. Rates of change multiply along the chain.

manas.q: State the chain rule.

children.note: For y = (3x + 1)², let u = 3x + 1. Then dy/du = 2u and du/dx = 3, so dy/dx = 6(3x + 1).
Backpropagation applies the chain rule from the loss back through each layer, reusing results so all gradients cost about as much as one extra forward pass.

manas.q: What is backpropagation?

children.note: Libraries like PyTorch and JAX record the operations you run and compute exact gradients for you. In PyTorch, loss.backward() fills in .grad for every parameter.

manas.q: What does loss.backward() do in PyTorch?

children.note: Multiplying many small factors through deep layers can shrink gradients to almost nothing, or many large ones can blow them up. Careful initialisation, normalisation and residual links help.

manas.q: What are vanishing gradients?

children.note: A loss function turns "how wrong is the model?" into one number that training tries to make small.
A loss maps the model's prediction and the true answer to a non-negative cost. Lower is better; zero means a perfect match.

manas.q: What is a loss function?

children.note: For predicting numbers: loss = average of (y − ŷ)². Squaring punishes big misses heavily, so outliers have a strong pull.

manas.q: What is the formula for mean squared error?

children.note: Loss = average of |y − ŷ|. It treats every unit of error the same, so it is less swayed by outliers than squared error.
For classification: loss = −log(probability the model gave the correct class). Confident wrong answers are punished very hard.

manas.q: Which loss is standard for classification and language models?

children.note: Accuracy is what people care about but it is not smooth, so it cannot guide gradients. We train on a smooth loss and report the metric separately.
Adding a penalty such as λ × (sum of squared weights) to the loss discourages over-complicated models and helps them generalise.
Gradient descent repeatedly steps against the gradient to lower the loss. Nearly every modern model is trained with a version of it.
w ← w − η × ∇L(w). Compute the gradient of the loss, take a small step the other way, repeat. η is the learning rate.

manas.q: Write the gradient descent update rule.

children.note: Imagine walking down a hill in thick fog. You cannot see the valley, but you can feel the slope under your feet and step downhill again and again.
Minimise L(w) = (w − 3)². The gradient is 2(w − 3). Start at w = 0 with η = 0.1: gradient −6, so w becomes 0.6, then about 1.08, creeping toward 3.
Full-batch uses all data per step, stochastic uses one example, mini-batch uses a small group. Mini-batches are the usual balance of speed and stability.

manas.q: What is mini-batch gradient descent?

children.note: One iteration is one update step. One epoch is one full pass over the training data, made of many mini-batch steps.
Momentum keeps a running average of past gradients to roll through small bumps. Adam also adapts the step size per parameter and is a common default.

manas.q: What does momentum add to plain gradient descent?

children.note: The learning rate is the step size, often the most important setting to tune.
Training is safe but painfully slow, and may stall before getting anywhere useful.
Steps overshoot the valley, so the loss bounces around or explodes to infinity or NaN.

manas.q: What happens if the learning rate is too large?

children.note: Many runs start with a short warm-up of small steps, then slowly decay the rate so training can settle into a good spot.
Try values like 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 and watch the loss curve. Good values differ between optimisers and models.
The loss surface of a big network is huge and bumpy. Knowing its features explains what can go wrong.
A global minimum is the lowest point anywhere; a local minimum is lowest only in its neighbourhood. Gradient descent can settle in a local one.

manas.q: What is the difference between a local and a global minimum?

children.note: A convex loss is bowl-shaped with only one minimum, so gradient descent will find it. Linear and logistic regression are convex; neural networks are not.

manas.q: Why is a convex loss easy to optimise?

children.note: A saddle point is flat in some directions and curves up in some and down in others. In high dimensions these and flat plateaus slow training more often than bad local minima.

manas.q: What is a saddle point?

children.note: In practice, very large networks usually reach low-loss regions that work well, and the noise from mini-batches helps escape poor spots. The full theory is still being studied.

children.topic: Low training loss is not the goal
children.note: A model can drive training loss near zero by memorising and still fail on new data (overfitting). Always watch validation loss too.
Steady fall is good; flat from the start suggests a bug or tiny learning rate; wild spikes suggest it is too high; widening train–validation gap suggests overfitting.
